parsed_answer.content: Designing a rate limiter in a distributed system requires balancing strict traffic regulation, low latency, and horizontal scalability. When designing this infrastructure component, we must evaluate three primary algorithmic paradigms: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window. The Token Bucket algorithm allows bursty traffic by accumulating tokens in a bucket up to a maximum capacity, consuming a token for every incoming request. This fits APIs where brief traffic spikes are legitimate. Conversely, the Leaky Bucket algorithm smooths out bursts entirely by queuing requests and processing them at a strictly constant, FIFO (First-In, First-Out) rate, preventing downstream saturation at the cost of increased tail latency. The Sliding Window algorithm—combining the memory efficiency of counters with the accuracy of sliding logs—prevents the boundary-burst exploit of fixed windows by tracking request timestamps across overlapping rolling time frames.

items: Distributed synchronization typically relies on Redis backed by Lua scripts. Running Lua guarantees atomicity for read-modify-write operations on token counts or window tallies without distributed locking bottlenecks.

In high-scale systems, relying purely on Redis for every request introduces network hops. Implementing a local in-memory cache with an eventually-consistent sliding window sync reduces network overhead while tolerating minor telemetry inaccuracies.

parsed_answer.content: Production Gotcha: Never rely on system clocks (System.currentTimeMillis()) across multiple nodes in a distributed cluster for sliding window or token refill calculations. Clock drift will cause inconsistent rate limiting. Always use Redis server time via EVALSHA with Redis TIME commands, or rely strictly on monotonic clocks (System.nanoTime()) for local thread-safe state.
